title: The Candle Problem and the Cash Prize
text:
The candle problem, invented by the psychologist Karl Duncker in the 1930s, is a simple puzzle. You are given a candle, a book of matches and a box of thumbtacks, and asked to fix the candle to a wall so that it can burn without dripping wax on the table. The solution is to empty the box, tack it to the wall and use it as a shelf for the candle. Most people take a while to see it, because they think of the box only as a container.

In 1962 Sam Glucksberg, then at New York University, tested how money affected people trying to solve it. Some participants were told they were simply helping to establish norms for how long the puzzle takes. Others were offered cash: five dollars if they were among the fastest quarter of participants and twenty dollars if they were the fastest of all.

When the tacks were inside the box, the offer of money made people slower to find the solution. But Glucksberg also ran an easier version in which the tacks lay on the table next to an empty box, which made the box's use obvious. In that version, the people offered money solved it faster.
lesson: Rewards help people go faster down a path they can already see, but can narrow their thinking when the answer requires seeing things in a new way.
source: Glucksberg, S. (1962). The influence of strength of drive on functional fixedness and perceptual recognition. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 63(1), 36-41.
